newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee coop data confirm cut in crop - grower.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee coop data confirm cut in crop - grower.

text.p: A sharp drop in coffee received by cooperatives in past months is proof this harvest is markedly lower and certainly not higher than last year as suggested by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, producers said.

"There is no way this crop can be bigger than last year. The market is not willing to recognise this and we have to be clear on this point," said Luis Hafers, vice-president of the growers' National Coffee Council (CNC).
This week the CNC said that 1.16 million 60-kg bags of coffee had been received by cooperatives during the month of July, bringing the total since May to 1.96 million bags.
This is down 30 percent from the 2.80 million bags delivered in the same period in 1996, with the 1996/97 crop now widely thought to have been between 25 million to 28 million bags.

However the 1997 deliveries still show a 100 percent increase on the 916,500 bags received during May to July 1995 when the frost and drought-hit 1996/97 crop, estimated at around 13 to 15 million bags, was being brought in.

Brazilian 1997/98 crop estimates range from 18 million bags by some producer officials to 28 million bags by the USDA, with the USDA plotting the current harvest as slightly higher than the 27.5 million bags it estimated was harvested in 1996/97.
The Brazilian government is working with a figure of 22 million bags while traders are happier around 24 million.
But while cooperative figures are illustrative, they are not used to gauge exact crop size as is the case in Colombia, traders said.

Moreover this year climatic conditions are leading to very irregular harvesting in that the numerous flowerings for the crop has led to many green beans still on the trees while the June rains also significantly delayed pickings.
As a result cooperatives may see a marked increase in coffee deliveries in the coming months, traders said.
"The cooperative figures are definitely an indication but this crop is coming in later than last year's," said Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Federation.
"It is too early in mid-August to talk about a 18 million to 20 million bag crop. Everything on a flux basis indicates we have between 22 million and 24 million bags," one dealer said.
Even with a 28 million bag crop, total demand in 1997/98 would still outstrip production, traders said.

With exports of green beans estimated at 15 million bags (allowing for Brazil being given the same export allowance at an upcoming meeting of producing countries), exports of soluble coffee accounting for 2.2 million and internal demand at 11.5 million bags, this gives a total of 28.7 million bags.

Working with an estimate of 24 million bags, this becomes an even bigger deficit of 4.7 million bags. With government stocks at 12.19 million bags, around 39 percent of the stockpile would be needed to fill the gap, traders said.

This week the Sao Paulo State Coffee Industry Union once again called on the government to increase the size of its monthly sales to ease current supply problems for domestic roasters, arguing also this was an ideal time for the government to offload its stocks and not compete with fellow producers.
"At this point, only Brazil has stocks to sell and should do so when it will not be competing with Colombian and Central American stocks," the union said in a statement.
